text_narrative: Halfway through the afternoon run the balls on the tall governor sit lower than Maret likes. She stands under the arms with a rag in one hand and watches the sleeve. The right ball hangs a finger below its fellow, and the arm carrying it shows a bright line where the pin works in the eye. The sleeve rides down, the throttle link tightens, and the wheel takes more water than the shop has any use for.
text_nonnarrative: Droop is classed by the difference between the two balls and never by the height of the sleeve alone. An arm with a worn pin in its eye is a fault of the linkage and falls outside the class. Bright metal at a joint bears on the cause and never on the grade. Throttle position at the time of grading is immaterial, and the water the wheel takes is a consequence rather than a criterion.

text_narrative: Everyone at the lower works had a theory about the third turbine, and the fitters had the worst of them. It ran two points down on the same head as its neighbours, and the men blamed the shaft, the coupling, and the water itself. Old Rusko went in through the manhole with a candle and came out saying the guide vanes were feathered thin at the trailing edge, every one of them, like a row of worn quills.
text_nonnarrative: The vanes stood in a ring about the runner, each pivoted on its own spindle in the head cover. Their angle was the single variable of the machine, and the flow through the runner was a function of that angle and of the head above it. Wear at the trailing edge was a matter of the water rather than of the setting. Without a tight ring, vanes and runner were mechanically independent at any gate position.

text_narrative: There was a valve-keeper on the high pipe who never trusted the surge chamber, and the hill under it never trusted him. Twice a year he shut the wheel gate quick, to hear the column knock, and the water in the shaft climbed and dropped and settled as the builders had promised. On the third autumn the shaft answered late. He shut the gate at noon and the knock arrived at dusk, from further up the hill than any pipe ran.
text_nonnarrative: Three provisions against surge are distinguished by what each does with the excess. An open standpipe holds it as height; a surge chamber holds it as a mass of water free to oscillate; a relief valve keeps none of it and passes the excess to waste. The first two are alike in returning water to the pipe, and the third is not. Depth of the shaft, not diameter, separates the chamber from the standpipe, and neither bears on the valve.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the diverted river the commissioners of the eastern cut ordered the headrace shortened by ninety yards. The masons took the old sill out in a week. At the autumn gauging the level in the tailrace stood higher than the drawings allowed, and the fall across the works was less by a foot than in the year before. The clerk entered the figure twice, once in the ledger and once on the wall.
text_nonnarrative: The headrace lay straight for a quarter mile above the works, its banks turfed on the field side and stone-faced toward the river. The tailrace was the wider of the two channels and the shallower. Between them the fall was some eleven feet at ordinary water, and rather less in flood. Ground on the northern bank stood higher than the sill, and the meadow beyond it was the wetter of the two grounds in any season.

text_narrative: The drill in the third bay slows again, and Verity does not need the gauge to know it. Sixty pounds, maybe less. Somebody on the floor above has put a second hoist on the same branch, and there is nothing in the standing orders against it, which is the whole difficulty. She sets the tool down. The trouble is not the compressor, whatever the engineer's report says; the trouble is a main sized for a smaller shop.
text_nonnarrative: Consumption varied more between shops on one main than between mains. The median draw of a hand drill was of the order of twenty cubic feet a minute, and hoists accounted for most of the spread. Pressure at the far bays was some fifteen pounds below the receiver in nine cases of ten. Age of a main was a poorer predictor of that drop than the number of branches taken off it within the same shop.

text_narrative: Since the family left, the house pump had not been worked, but the copper vessel above it was warm when Ondre put a hand to it in the dark. He moved the handle twice and waited. Water came, without the knock a dry pump makes, and the vessel breathed under his palm as though a second hand rested on the other side of the copper and pressed back at the same slow and patient rate.
text_nonnarrative: Charged with air and closed at its crown, the vessel above a force pump is a chamber whose whole duty is the evening out of an intermittent delivery. Its cushion is a body of trapped air, compressed on the pressure stroke and expanded again between strokes. Capacity is therefore modest and fixed by the swept volume of the barrel. A vessel with no air in it is dead space and has no such property at all.

text_narrative: Nobody at the brewery boiler house will stand a valve set by ear, and the reason goes back to the winter the second boiler lost its plug. Kell does it with the dead weight and the long lever and a hook scale, every valve, twice over. He will tell anyone who lingers that a valve which lifts at the right pressure and then refuses to seat again is worse than one that never lifts at all.
text_nonnarrative: Every boiler above a stated pressure was required to carry two valves of the direct-loaded kind, of which one was to be beyond the reach of the house. Lever and weight were permitted only where the weight was fixed and stamped with the pressure. Seating pressure was to lie within a twentieth of the lifting pressure. A valve adjustable by hand from the working floor was not admissible, whatever its size and whatever its setting.

text_narrative: There was a keeper of the deep furnaces who trusted nothing she could not empty and fill again. Twice in every watch she cracked the bottom cock of the gauge glass and let the water fall out of it, and twice she let it back. The other keepers laughed at her for it, until the season the glass in the eastern house showed a steady half and the boiler under it was dry as a bell.
text_nonnarrative: A gauge glass is the least trustworthy honest instrument in a boiler house, and the reason is structural: a steady reading is what a blocked passage and a correct level have in common. Blowdown is worth its interruption because it tells the two apart, and nothing else does. The objection that frequent blowdown wears the cocks is sound as far as it goes, and it does not touch the case for blowing them at all.

text_narrative: In the second winter of the works the north battery lost its heater for eleven days. The engineer on duty recorded a fall of nine degrees in the feed and a leak of four gallons an hour at the front tube plate. Two tubes were plugged on the ninth day and a third on the tenth. The plate itself was recorded sound. The heater was returned to service at reduced feed and the entry was countersigned.
text_nonnarrative: A heater was condemned on the state of its tube plate and never on the number of tubes plugged. A leak at the plate counted against the heater whatever the gallons lost, while the same leak in a tube body was a matter for that tube alone. Degrees of rise in the feed bore on the duty and not on the class. Return to service at reduced feed was no part of the grading.

text_narrative: The siphon over the wall had run for nine years, and now it would not, and Osred stood at the crest with the plug out and no notion why. Full of water, both legs. That was the thing. A siphon which had lost its prime showed air at the crown, and this one showed none, and the level in the upper cistern was exactly where it should be, and the lower cistern had not been touched since spring.
text_nonnarrative: Prime: the condition of a siphon whose bore is full of liquid throughout, with no free surface between the two legs. Air lock: any pocket of gas at or near the crown large enough to divide the column. Break-off: the height above the upper surface at which a column of the liquid cannot be supported. Crest: the highest point of the bore, and the usual seat of an air lock in a siphon of long span.

text_narrative: Forty cocks are set into the service tunnel under the dome, and Ilva carries three keys for them, which is two fewer than the schedule allows. The eighteenth cock takes none of the three. She kneels on the grating with the lamp between her knees and turns the smallest key over in the light: the square is right, the throat is right, the depth is short by the width of a fingernail.
text_nonnarrative: A key meant, in this part, an implement of square socket intended to bear on the plug of a stopcock and on nothing else. Where a cock lay beneath a public footway, only a key of the long pattern applied to it. A socket true in square but short in depth was not a key within the meaning of this part. Nothing in the schedule of patterns affected the duty to maintain the plug.

text_narrative: Nobody at the river station would say who had left the back panel off the third switchboard, and the inspector was not a man who asked twice. He put his lamp along the bars and found the cause of the flicker in the west of the town at the far end of the frame: a strip of brass shim laid across the gap between two phases, cut square, and forgotten there by whoever dressed the joint.
text_nonnarrative: Two sections stand coupled only where both are dead or both are alive at one voltage and one phase rotation. A board on which a section is fed from two sides at once is barred, and the bar holds whatever the load. Shim, packing and any loose metal between bars of differing phase are not a condition of the board but a defect in it, and no setting of the switches answers them at all.

text_narrative: There was a lamp-wright in the low country who kept her fuse wire in a drawer of nine compartments, and she would not let a stranger choose from it. The thinnest was for the shrine lamps that burned all night and drew nothing. The thickest she used twice in her life. A traveller who took the third from the left for a hall of forty lamps walked home in the dark, three times in one winter.
text_nonnarrative: Nine gauges made up the drawer, of which the fourth and fifth were the ones in daily use. Each was a tinned wire on its own card, the card marked with a nominal current and with the size of the copper it protected. The thinnest was of the order of a hair and lay under a glass lid. Two spare cards of the commonest gauge sat at the back of every drawer in the shop.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the pumping station the directors called for cards from every cylinder on a single day. The engineman took twenty-two of them between six and noon at a steady load, and the draughtsman traced them all onto one sheet. Four cards showed a toe rounded where the others showed a corner. Three of the four belonged to the oldest engine. The sheet was bound into the minute book and nothing was ordered.
text_nonnarrative: What passes for engine analysis in the trade is usually card-reading of a slack kind: area is taken for power and shape for the health of the valve gear, and the second inference is far weaker than the first. A rounded toe is read as late admission by habit rather than by argument or measurement. The best practitioners of the form are those who date every card, name the engine, and distrust a single sheet.

text_narrative: The engine in the empty house is hunting again, and Tarrow counts the swings from the yard because the door is not one he intends to open. Eight to the minute, perhaps nine. Faster than yesterday, and wider. A governor hunts because the load shifts under it, that is the whole of what a governor does, and there has been no load in that house since the wheel was uncoupled in the spring and the belt taken off.
text_nonnarrative: Disagreement over whether hunting is a fault of a governor or a property of the whole loop turns on what is meant by fault. On one account the governor is the seat of the defect, since a governor with more friction in its sleeve does not hunt. On the other the oscillation belongs to no part, being a relation between the response of the engine and the delay in the linkage. The second account is harder to state and more general.

text_narrative: At first light the conduit master came up the hill road with a staff and a knotted cord, and measured the fall from the spring house to the town cistern for the third time that month. Eighty-one feet. The cistern stood dry at midday all the same. At the fourth arch he laid his ear against the lead and heard the water going fast and thin, faster than eighty-one feet of fall could account for.
text_nonnarrative: Loss of head in a straight main is very nearly proportional to the square of the mean velocity and to the length, and inversely to the diameter. The coefficient is a property of the bore and of its roughness rather than of the water. At very low velocities the square law fails and the loss tends toward a simple proportion. Fall available and loss are equal in a main running full and free at delivery.

text_narrative: Everybody on the terrace bought mantles from the ironmonger on the corner, and everybody complained about them, and nobody went elsewhere. The trick, as the old women had it, was in the first burning. Sela lit her mantle with the glass off and the door shut, and the ash held its shape for a year and more. Her sister lit two in a draught and both went to powder at the crown inside a week.
text_nonnarrative: A mantle is graded on the state of its crown and on nothing below the shoulder. Ash gone to powder at the crown is disqualifying whatever the light the mantle gives and whatever its age. A draught during the burning bears on the cause and never on the class. Shape held for a week counts for nothing; the class is set by shape held under the glass at working heat, and by that alone.

text_narrative: There was a wind in the eastern marshes that would not be faced, and the fen-folk built their pumps with eight-vaned fantails against it. The oldest pump had six. It stood with its face to the north through every wind of that country and pumped nothing for a hundred years. In the year the marsh dried, the six vanes came round of themselves, and the mill faced east, and no water lay under it to lift.
text_nonnarrative: The fantail was a small wheel of six or eight flat vanes set on a spindle at right angles to the main sails. Its spindle bore a worm, and the worm engaged a rack about the curb. The vanes were flat boards, never twisted, and each was housed in a spider of iron arms. On the smallest pumps the spider was absent and the vanes were framed direct onto the boss of the spindle.

text_narrative: In the ninth year of the harbour works the great crane on the north quay was taken down and its drum measured. The wheel proved to be eighteen feet across the treads and the drum four, which no ledger in the town had recorded. Two of the six spokes were sound. The pawl and its ratchet were laid aside for the smith, and the rest of the timber was sold where it lay.
text_nonnarrative: Wheel, drum and shaft are one assembly in a treadwheel crane: the treads are boards fixed inside the rim, and the drum sits on the same shaft, inboard of the wheel. A pawl stands over a ratchet at the drum end and is the only part out of the line of the shaft. The jib is separate. In smaller cranes the second wheel is absent and the shaft rests on two bearings only.

text_narrative: Four hundred miles from the depot and the delivery valve on the water pump would not hold. Sennen had grit of a sort, the fine grey dust off the lake bed, worked into tallow. It was not lapping powder and she knew it. She worked the disc on its seat by thumb for an hour by the watch, dry-lipped, thinking about the eight days of pumping between the camp and the next open water.
text_nonnarrative: A lift valve of this kind has four parts and no more: a disc, a seat ring set into the body, a guide, and a light spring above. The disc bears on the seat along a narrow annular face, and that face is the whole of the joint. Guide and disc are one piece in the smaller sizes. Grit between the two faces is no part of the valve, though the lapping of them depends on it.

text_narrative: The lamp over the loading bay burns short again and Corvin goes up the ladder with the case of carbons under one arm. Vacuum outside, atmosphere in here, and the arc still eats an inch an hour. He racks the stub out of the lower holder. The case has four sizes in it and only the second fits the upper clip, and eleven of the second are left in the whole station.
text_nonnarrative: Four sizes made up the standard case: three plain carbons of increasing diameter and one cored. The cored size was the commonest, its core a soft paste that held the arc central. Each stick was some twelve inches long, square-ended, with a copper skin over all but the last inch. The smallest was stocked in quantity and the largest in twos, being wanted for the yard lamps and for nothing else.

text_narrative: Nobody in the machine house lets the new men near the dynamos on a Monday, and Halvard is the reason, or the story about Halvard is. He beds brushes by feel and he is never wrong about it, and he will not be told that a strip of glass paper round the commutator is quicker. Three minutes with the paper, he says, and three weeks of sparking at the heel of every brush.
text_nonnarrative: Much of what the trade called brush-setting was really brush-forcing, and the fault lay in the standard of proof: a brush free of sparking under load was held to be bedded, whatever the state of its heel. Glass paper was defended on the ground that it was quick, which was true and beside the point. The soundest men were those who judged a brush by its face and not by the machine's behaviour.

text_narrative: There was a heron who nested in the third bend of the hot main where it crossed the marsh, and she chose it because the iron there was never quite still. In the cold months the bend drew back and her nest sat over open water. In the heat it pushed out and the nest lay over reed. A young otter told her the pipe was straight and she should shift. She stayed nine summers.
text_nonnarrative: Nothing in the geometry of an expansion loop settles whether it is a kind of joint or simply a length of pipe. On the first view its duty is to absorb movement, its virtue is compliance, and it belongs with bellows and slip couplings. On the second, its behaviour follows from ordinary bending and there is nothing peculiar about it. The second view explains more and surrenders a distinction between a main and its fittings.

text_narrative: In the year the second mill was raised the founders cast the flywheel in six segments and joined them at the arms with cotters and links. The rim measured twenty-two feet and the wheel was worked at forty turns to the minute for eleven seasons. At the autumn survey a cotter at the fourth joint was found slack by a quarter inch. The wheel was slowed to thirty turns and the entry stood unaltered.
text_nonnarrative: Hoop stress in a rim went as the square of the rim speed and was independent of the radius at a given speed, so that a large wheel and a small one at equal rim speed stood equally stressed. The constant was a property of the metal alone. Joints in a segmented rim took none of that stress directly, and the bolts at a joint were sized on the arm loads instead.

text_narrative: The second lift of the holder is up at seven in the morning and the town has burned nothing since Friday. Idra watches the crown from the office window and does the arithmetic twice. Gas from where. The cups are full, the grips are dry, the guide rollers sit true in their standards, and the holder rises a foot a day out of a main that runs to nowhere at all and never has.
text_nonnarrative: A holder was condemned on the seal at its cups and grips, never on the height of a lift. A crown out of level counted as one class of defect and rollers off their standards as a second, the two being independent. Gas in the main bore on the cause and not at all on the class. Rise of a foot in a day was no evidence either way, being a matter of the works.

text_narrative: Three sets run in the converter house at the northern depot and only two are needed on a weekday. At half past four this afternoon the middle set drops out of step and the board goes over to the standby without a flicker on the line. The attendant records a bearing temperature nine degrees above the others and shuts the set down. No traffic is delayed and the depot works the evening peak on two machines.
text_nonnarrative: One armature serves both machines in a rotary converter: it sits in a single field, with slip rings at one end and a commutator at the other. Alternating supply at the rings and direct output at the commutator are two aspects of the same winding rather than two circuits. Speed is fixed by the supply frequency and by the number of poles, and by nothing else. Without the rings the machine is an ordinary motor.

text_narrative: Before the cold was given its own name, the makers set a small brass gate at the foot of every pipe in the world and told it one thing: hold what is hot, pass what is cold. The gate was honest and slow. Water went through it and steam did not, and the makers were satisfied. But the gate could never tell cold water from cold steam, and there is a house in the north still emptying.
text_nonnarrative: Traps fall into three classes by what each of them senses. A float trap answers to the level of condensate and is indifferent to temperature. A thermostatic trap answers to temperature and is indifferent to level. A thermodynamic trap belongs with neither, since it depends on the velocity of flashing water across a disc and senses no state of the condensate at all. Orifice size separates duties within a class and never separates the classes themselves.

text_narrative: Every dry month Weir walks the bund of the old cooling pond. In the first month he finds the north arms still turning on their own head, and he leaves them alone. In the third he wires up two nozzles that spray sideways into the reeds. In the sixth the pond is down a foot and the spray falls short of the water, and he walks the bund twice that month and does nothing.
text_nonnarrative: The pond lay in a shallow rectangle east of the plant, its bund some four feet above the water at ordinary level. Two rows of spray arms stood over it on trestles, the northern row nearer the bund than the southern. Reed beds occupied the eastern third of the water. The bottom shelved from a foot at the margin to seven near the outfall, and the western side was the deeper throughout.

text_narrative: Each week of the survey took Bregt to a different settlement standpipe. At the first the float was a sealed copper ball and the gear read true. At the fourth the ball had a pinhole and sat two inches low, and the whole village drew from a tower it believed to be half full. At the ninth there was no float at all, only a boy on the ladder with a chalk mark.
text_nonnarrative: Error in the indicated level varied more between towers of one pattern than between patterns. The median discrepancy was some two inches, and floats with any breach in them accounted for most of the spread. Attendants at the larger towers reported the gear as trustworthy in nine cases of ten, and the sample of smaller towers was too thin to bear a figure at all, whatever the pattern of the gear.

text_narrative: A ram at the foot of the hospital garden was found still beating on the morning of the third, eleven days after the drive pipe above it had been cut for the new road. The gardener reported the beat as regular, at some sixty to the minute. The delivery tank was full and the overflow running. No connection to the upper spring could be traced by the two men sent out, and the beat continued.
text_nonnarrative: Among pumps that use no outside power, the hydraulic ram is the one that works on the momentum of its own supply. A long drive pipe, a waste valve at its foot and a delivery valve into an air vessel are the whole of it. Delivery height is a large multiple of the fall, and the delivered fraction correspondingly small. Beat rate depends on the length of the drive pipe and on the waste valve setting.

text_narrative: In the first age of the deep engines the smiths packed every gland with rope of hemp and tallow, and the water they held back was not water. Each box took nine turns of it, cut on the skew, with the joints of the turns set a third of a circle apart. The last smith to pack a gland in the old way went down to the sixth level with a coil on her shoulder.
text_nonnarrative: Packing was to be of square section, cut on the skew, and laid in rings of one turn each with the joints staggered by a third of a circle. Six turns were required in a box of ordinary depth and nine where the pressure stood above a stated figure. Hemp was permitted only below a stated temperature. A gland drawn hard enough to prevent all leakage was not acceptable on any shaft in motion.

text_narrative: The pacing machine at the winter track runs off a flat belt, and Nolwenn dresses it before each meeting. On the first night she uses too much and the belt grips hard and the rider behind it complains of a jerk out of the banking. On the third she uses none and loses four seconds to slip in the last mile. On the fifth she splits the difference and nobody says anything.
text_nonnarrative: Slip in a flat belt was a safeguard and not a loss, and the trade was slow to say so. A belt incapable of slipping transmitted every shock in the load straight into the shafting, and the shafting had no other relief. The objection was that slip wasted power, and it did waste power, at some two parts in a hundred. That cost bought a margin no other part of the drive supplied.

text_narrative: Three times on the southern passage the vacuum in the main condenser fell away, and each time Odhran was sent below to find it. The first time it was the air pump, out of stroke on one side. The second it was a joint at the gland of the exhaust, whistling faintly. The third time the gauge showed twenty-four inches and every joint was tight, and the sea outside was warmer than the chart allowed.
text_nonnarrative: Vacuum is classed by the seat of a loss and not by its depth. An air pump out of stroke is one class; a leaking joint at a gland or in the exhaust is a second, and the two are graded apart however alike the gauge reads. Sea temperature bears on the cause and never on the class, since warm water is no defect in a condenser. Inches of vacuum fix degree within a class.

text_narrative: Twice at the change of shift the ring main on the third habitat level knocks, and the duty engineer logs it as a slam at the outfall valve. Pressure at the far gauge touches nine hundred and returns. No pipe is displaced and no joint shows wet. A second knock at the same hour the following day is logged with a note that the valve is now closing in eleven seconds instead of two.
text_nonnarrative: Slam: the shock in a main proper to too-rapid closure of a valve, reckoned as a rise above the working pressure. Column separation: the condition of a water column parted from itself at a high point, with a void between the parts. Rejoinder: the second and usually larger shock, peculiar to a separated column. Surge: any pressure change of the same family slow enough to be measured in seconds rather than in fractions.

text_narrative: When the sky was first strung, the makers gave each pole three cups of glass, one under the other, so that the rain of the world would find no road down the wood. The rain accepted this. In the country of long mists it sent no rain at all and laid its water on the glass from beneath, and the poles there were given a fourth cup, turned upward, and they stand taller in the west.
text_nonnarrative: An insulator meant, in this part, a body of glass or glazed clay interposed between a conductor and its support, having not fewer than two sheds. A shed meant any downward skirt whose under surface stood clear of the body. Where a line lay in a district of salt air, three sheds were required and a fourth was permitted. Nothing in this part affected the sizing of the pin or of the crossarm.

text_narrative: Sera keeps six substations alive along the coast road and each one teaches her something about horn gaps. At the first the horns are set wide and the arrester has never once flashed over. At the third they are set close and it flashes in clear weather. At the fifth somebody before her filed the points to needles. At the sixth there are no horns, only two lengths of fence wire.
text_nonnarrative: A gap is admissible only where its setting lies below the withstand of the apparatus behind it and above the crest of the working voltage. A station in which the earth resistance exceeds the stated figure counts as unprotected, whatever the gap. Filed or pointed horns are not a setting and cannot be answered by any adjustment. Two arresters on one line at differing settings are barred as a position.

text_narrative: The city was given its water pressure by seven towers, and each tower held a weight, and each weight was said to be the patience of the district beneath it. The tower in the glass quarter held the smallest, and its cranes were the quickest in the port. The tower over the salt flats held two hundred tons and shifted a hand's breadth in a year, and that district never hurried at anything.
text_nonnarrative: Three patterns of accumulator are found in a works of any size. The smallest is a plain ram in an open frame, loaded with cast weights on a crosshead, and it is the commonest. The middle pattern is the weighted tower proper, a ram in a case filled with slag or gravel. The largest is a differential accumulator with two rams of unequal diameter, rare and kept for high pressures alone.

text_narrative: The lighting plant behind the freight office at the cattle stop was reported dead on the morning of the eleventh, four months after the last train of the season. An electrician up from the junction found thirty cells standing at less than a volt and the positive plates white to the edge. The shed was dry and the connections clean. The plant had been left charged and unattended, which the company book allowed.
text_nonnarrative: Much of the battery practice of the period rested on a false comfort: a plant standing idle was thought to be a plant at rest, when idleness was the one condition under which sulphation was certain. Company books that allowed months of standing without charge were the visible form of the error. What was called neglect in the tender was usually compliance. The best houses treated a full cell as a thing needing work.

text_narrative: The first shaft was a single length of iron laid along the roof of the world, and it turned everything. When it wore, the smiths cut it and set a hanger at the cut, and it was two shafts that turned as one. They cut it again and again, until the roof was a hundred lengths in a hundred bearings, and nobody in the shops below could say where one shaft ended.
text_nonnarrative: Counting the shafts in a mill is not a matter of counting the couplings. On one criterion a line of shafting is a single object, because it has one angular velocity throughout and no part of it is free of the rest. On another it is many, since each length has its own bearings, its own deflection and its own history. Neither criterion is idle, and the disagreement is about objects rather than words.

text_narrative: At ten minutes to three the night chart from the river substation shows a second peak, as high as the evening one and half an hour wide. The district it feeds is four streets of shuttered warehouses and a bonded store. Nothing on the schedule accounts for it. The recorder is checked against the station meters and agrees with them to within a hundred units, and the same peak is on last night's chart.
text_nonnarrative: Peak demand stood in rough proportion to the number of consumers, while the diversity factor diminished with it, so that the sum of the individual maxima always lay well above the maximum of the sum. Load factor was the ratio of the mean to the peak over a day and rarely exceeded a third on a lighting supply. Beyond a certain size of district the diversity factor was near enough constant.
